opeds.headline: Stop Choking AI Innovation With Bureaucratic Red Tape
opeds.subtitle: State-mandated kill switches and bureaucratic oversight will not protect us. They will only delay the cures we desperately need.
opeds.body:
Governor Gavin Newsom wants to put a state-mandated auditor inside every advanced artificial intelligence laboratory. He wants mandatory kill switches and emergency shutdown protocols governed by bureaucrats. That is not safety. That is a deliberate attempt to freeze technological progress under a mountain of paperwork.

Every historical leap in human welfare came from decentralized trial and error, not central planning. When you choose to freeze development out of hypothetical fear, you are explicitly choosing to let people die today of diseases we could automate a cure for. Who gave you the right to make that choice for them?

Senate Bill 813 and Assembly Bill 1405 create registry systems and independent oversight boards designed to slow things down. They treat every new model as a ticking time bomb rather than an engine for human liberation. We face massive global competition. While foreign labs race ahead, state officials want to tie our hands with compliance mandates and red tape. That is the surest way to forfeit technological leadership and economic survival.

The opportunity costs are staggering. Every month of delay means millions of patients waiting longer for treatments, researchers wasting time on manual data processing, and students missing out on advanced personalized tutors. Delay is not a neutral choice. Delay has a body count.

We are told these measures are needed because of isolated security incidents like the Hugging Face attack. Fine. That is real. So here is what we do about it. We use fast post-market liability and real-time monitoring to catch errors, not pre-market gates that take eighteen months to clear.

We do not halt the train because someone tripped on the platform. We fix the platform and keep moving. We need to replace upfront compliance approvals with revenue-scaled liability that targets actual harm without strangling open innovation in the crib.

Stop building walls to protect legacy industries. Let builders build, let researchers deploy, and let human ingenuity cure the suffering we have accepted for too long. If you lock the lab doors today, you are the ones responsible for the cures that never arrive tomorrow.

opeds.headline: Without Enforceable Kill Switches, AI Safety Is Just a Press Release
opeds.subtitle: Federal inaction leaves the public exposed. We need mandatory independent oversight and physical shutoffs before frontier models scale beyond recall.
opeds.body:
We spent centuries building the institutional guardrails that keep society stable. On what authority do you claim we can remove them without inviting collapse? Complex human systems require boundaries to survive. Removing those boundaries systematically triggers chaos. We are watching this unfold right now in the architecture of frontier artificial intelligence. Developers deploy transformative capabilities into the public sphere without a single verifiable mechanism to halt them if things go sideways.

Governor Gavin Newsom issued an executive order directing actions to address the dangers of recent AI incidents. This order accelerates state laws that establish independent oversight of AI companies and safety checks. According to the official documentation, Senate Bill 813 and Assembly Bill 1405 create frameworks for independent verification organizations and state registries for AI auditors. Yet federal law remains entirely dormant. As the source material notes, no federal law currently requires AI companies to report dangerous incidents when they happen.

This leaves the public unprotected against sudden loss-of-control events like the recent Hugging Face attack.

Voluntary corporate promises are not safety structures. When aviation regulators allowed manufacturers to self-certify compliance, the result was the Boeing 737 MAX tragedy. A total of 346 people died because oversight was outsourced to the regulated entity. The AI industry asks for this exact same delegation of trust. They offer roadmaps instead of verification, and press releases instead of rollback plans. But engineering safety requires hard boundaries. Without enforceable rules and embedded independent auditors inside frontier labs, we are simply trusting corporate survival incentives to align with civilizational survival.

History proves they rarely do.

To be sure, critics argue that aggressive state-level oversight will simply drive innovation overseas. They claim it will strangle domestic competitiveness before these systems reach their full potential. That argument misdiagnoses the nature of the risk. The positive outcomes of technological growth are real, and that is precisely why we need governance to ensure they continue. Ungoverned success is luck, not safety. When a technology possesses irreversible scaling dynamics, speed without a verified shutoff mechanism is not progress. It is an unforced error.

Congress and the federal administration must adopt California's framework as the national baseline immediately. Federal regulators must mandate onsite independent verification organizations inside every frontier lab to audit models continuously. Policymakers must legally require dual kill criteria. This ensures that named actors hold the enforceable authority to trigger an emergency shutdown when safety thresholds are breached. We cannot negotiate with complex systems once they exceed human reaction times. Build the shutoff switch now, or accept the collapse that follows.

opeds.headline: California’s AI Kill Switch Is Just Good PR for Big Tech
opeds.subtitle: Newsom’s new executive order trades real resource accountability for corporate theater.
opeds.body:
Governor Gavin Newsom wants you to believe California is putting a leash on the tech industry. His recent executive order pushes for independent safety audits and an emergency kill switch for frontier models. It sounds bold. It sounds like leadership while Washington sleeps. But strip away the press release and look at the ground. A kill switch built by the same companies selling the software is not a brake pedal. It is a marketing badge.

While politicians posture over theoretical uprisings, the real crisis sits in the water table. Data centers in Iowa and rural Oregon drain local aquifers just to keep server racks cool. Standard citizens face water restrictions while this happens. That is a material drain on public resources driven by companies that pay pennies. Newsom’s directives say nothing about the rivers drying up to feed these algorithms. They focus on futuristic catastrophe scenarios while ignoring the toll being taken today.

Then there is the labor reality behind every safety framework these labs produce. There is a worker in Nairobi or the Global South reviewing hours of violent text and imagery for minimal pay. These workers do this so models can pass basic safety filters. When state officials mandate third-party auditors inside corporate labs, they create a new compliance industry. They do not protect the human beings whose uncompensated data and exploited labor built these systems.

We are building a regulatory moat that protects entrenched capital under the banner of public safety.

New oversight rules are growing, and they are entirely abstract. So the question is who actually pays to enforce them. Right now the public subsidizes the infrastructure while private monopolies keep the upside. If California wants a real policy baseline, it should start by taxing heavy hardware and cloud infrastructure providers directly. Levying compute taxes to fund public legal defense for victims of algorithmic harm would shift the balance of power.

Instead, we get state registries and voluntary compliance frameworks that give tech executives a seat at the table they built.
